title: Getting a Job: How to Crash and Burn in Tech Interviews (Guest Post)
author: Brian Cullinan
summary: Guest wisdom from EBSCO AVP Roger Rohweder on how tech candidates spectacularly blow job interviews by sending generic resumes, lacking basic eye contact, and failing to research the company.
content_html:
Getting a Job: How to Crash and Burn in Tech Interviews

Published on November 25, 2008 by Brian Cullinan (featuring Roger Rohweder)

A visual guide to the brutal lifecycle of entry-level technical interviews.

This week I'm sharing insights from Roger Rohweder, Assistant Vice President at EBSCO Industries, who recently watched a fresh Computer Science graduate completely implode during a tech support interview.

How to Guarantee You Won't Get Hired

  • The Generic Blast Resume: Submitting an uncustomized, generic resume with no cover letter signals instantly that you applied to 400 positions in an automated batch run without caring about this specific job.
  • Mumbling in the Corner: Being soft-spoken in a mousy, hyper-geeky way does not work when applying for roles that require communicating with real humans or running customer training sessions.
  • Expecting Mind Reading: Coming to an interview expecting the hiring manager to figure out your skill set for you, rather than actively demonstrating what problems you can solve.
    • Faking Competence: Trying to fake knowledge when asked about a technology you don't know. The interviewer is an expert and will instantly smell the desperation.

The Bare Minimum Requirements

Do basic background research on the company, look the interviewer in the eye, ask insightful questions about their technical stack, and write a follow-up email making your case. It is incredible how low the bar is, yet candidates still manage to trip over it.
modern_insight_2026: Back in 2008, failing an interview meant mumbling in a conference room and sending an uncustomized PDF. In 2026, candidates get rejected by automated AI ATS screeners before a human ever reads their resume, and then face 5 rounds of LeetCode hard problems just to land a junior tech support role.

title: Hack of the Week: Bypassing Campus Network Throttling with SSH & Local SOCKS Tunnels
author: Brian Cullinan
summary: Routing local browser traffic through an encrypted SSH tunnel bound to port 1337 to bypass university WebSense filters, bandwidth throttling, and firewall inspection.
content_html:
Hack of the Week: Bypassing Campus Network Throttling with SSH & Local SOCKS Tunnels

Published on November 5, 2008 by Brian Cullinan

Tunneling encrypted traffic through custom ports to defeat university firewalls.

Campus network administrators love deploying WebSense content filters and throttling common proxy ports like 3128 and 8080. Here is how to route all your browser traffic through an encrypted SSH tunnel and bypass their oppressive rules entirely.

The Circumvention Blueprint

  1. Server Setup: Spin up a basic Squid proxy on a remote Ubuntu box.
  2. Port Evasion: Configure PuTTY to establish an SSH tunnel mapping local port 1337 directly to localhost:3128 on the remote box—dodging standard proxy port inspection.
  3. Browser Re-routing: Set Firefox's connection settings to forward HTTP traffic through localhost:1337.

Sure, encryption adds a slight overhead latency, but watching blocked sites load at un-throttled speeds right past campus IT security makes it totally worth it.
modern_insight_2026: Binding an unencrypted Squid proxy over SSH on port 1337 was classic 2000s script-kiddie gold. Today's enterprise deep packet inspection (DPI) and Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) engines would flag and terminate an un-whitelisted SSH tunnel in milliseconds.
